context.title: Values and bindings
context.objective: Trace a numeric reassignment and distinguish a value from its type.
context.body: Quoted numeric text is a string. The number 12 and the string "12" are different values. typeof returns a type description. A binding is a name for a value.

rubric: Accurate, grounded in the supplied reviewed reference and useful for a beginner; at most 180 words, plain text and readable code.

Explain why looking numeric does not make quoted text a number; distinguish value and type without inventing conversion rules or claiming learner confusion.

reply.text:
A binding acts as a label for a value. You create one using the let keyword followed by a name, an equals sign, and the value you want to store.

let score = 25;
console.log(typeof score); // "number"

In this example, the name score is bound to the numeric value 25. The typeof operator checks the type of the value currently held by that binding. Because 25 is a number, the result is "number".

If you later write score = 30;, the binding score now points to the value 30 instead of 25. The value itself is distinct from the name used to reference it. A string like "25" is a different value than the number 25, even if they look similar. You can always use typeof to confirm which category a value belongs to.

context.title: Functions and return values
context.objective: Follow arguments into a function and distinguish returning a value from logging it.
context.body:
A function packages reusable work. A parameter names an input inside the function. An argument is the value supplied when calling it. Each call to addFive gives minutes the supplied argument.

return sends a value back to the caller and ends that function call. console.log displays a value; it does not make an enclosing function return that value. An ordinary function that reaches its end without returning a value returns undefined, not null.

In the example, addFive(10) returns 15, which is stored in planned. A function containing only console.log("Ready") displays Ready but its caller receives undefined. These examples are read-only. Submitted JavaScript is never executed. Async functions and generators are outside this introduction.

context.title: Decisions with conditions
context.objective: Trace an if/else branch and distinguish strict equality from assignment.
context.body:
A comparison produces a boolean: true or false. The >= operator means greater than or equal to. An if statement executes its block when its condition is truthy; otherwise its else block executes. In this lesson all conditions are explicit boolean comparisons.

Use === to test strict equality. If the operands have different types, the result is false: 3 === "3" is false because a number and a string are different types. Assignment uses =; it does not test equality.

Trace the comparison before choosing a branch. With minutes = 20, the example prints Practice. With minutes = 10, the comparison 10 >= 15 is false, so only Review is printed. This introduction does not cover every truthy/falsy value or every numeric equality edge case.

context.title: Values and bindings
context.objective: Trace a numeric reassignment and distinguish a value from its type.
context.body:
A value is data, such as the number 3 or the string "Nexus". A binding gives a value a name. Use const when you will not reassign that binding; use let when you will. Assignment with = stores a new value in an existing mutable binding.

const prevents reassigning the binding, not changing the contents of an object. Here we use primitive values only. Quotes make "12" a string, while 12 without quotes is a number. typeof "12" produces the string "string"; typeof 12 produces "number".

Read the example from top to bottom. Both operands of + are numbers, so they are added. After score = score + 2, the new value of score is the number 2. The earlier value is replaced, not added to a separate history. String concatenation and object mutation are outside this introduction.

reply.text:
To trace this code, follow the execution line by line from the top. Keep a mental note of the current value stored in the binding.

When you see a let declaration, note the initial value assigned to the name. When you encounter an assignment statement using the = operator, calculate the expression on the right side first using the current value of the binding. Once you have that result, update the binding to hold this new value. The old value is discarded and no longer exists in that binding.

Compare the value before and after the assignment line to see how the binding has changed.
